title: Maximal Square
prompt: Given an `m x n` binary matrix `matrix` filled with 0s and 1s, find the largest square containing only 1s, and return its area.

examples.explanation: The largest all-1s square has side length 2, giving area 4.
With a single cell that is '0', no square of 1s exists at all, so the area is 0.

hints: Checking every possible square explicitly is expensive — instead think about what determines the largest square that can have its bottom-right corner at a given cell.
Define dp[r][c] as the side length of the largest all-1s square whose bottom-right corner is at (r, c). If matrix[r][c] is '0', dp[r][c] = 0.
If matrix[r][c] is '1', the square can only be as large as the smallest of its three neighbors (up, left, diagonal up-left) allow, plus one: dp[r][c] = min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1], dp[r-1][c-1]) + 1.

solution.approach: Define dp[r][c] as the side length of the largest square of all 1s whose bottom-right corner sits at (r, c). If matrix[r][c] is '0', no square can end there, so dp[r][c] = 0. If it's '1', extending a square to end at (r, c) requires ALL three of the square directly above, to the left, and diagonally above-left to already support a square of at least that size — the limiting neighbor caps how far the square can grow, so dp[r][c] = min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1], dp[r-1][c-1]) + 1 (treating out-of-bounds neighbors as 0, which naturally handles the first row/column). Track the maximum dp value seen; the answer is that maximum squared (side length to area).
